meta.title: Priority Pass — Puzzle Bank v1
meta.note: Scenarios 1-7 correspond to the original sample set discussed in planning (The Bait, Trigger Stacking, APNAP Politics, Order of Operations, Layers Check, The Fog Bluff, The Redundant Counter). Renumbered here for a consistent index across the full bank.

scenarios.title: The Bait
scenarios.board_state: You control Llanowar Elves and 3 untapped lands. You hold Counterspell. Opponent casts Concentrate (draw 3) at sorcery speed.

options.text: Counter the Concentrate
Pass priority, hold Counterspell
Respond by tapping Llanowar Elves for mana, then pass

scenarios.reveal: All three are legal, but B is generally correct: card draw isn't threatening enough to spend your only interaction on. The puzzle tests judgment, not legality.

scenarios.title: Trigger Stacking
scenarios.board_state: You control Blood Artist and Zulaport Cutthroat. A board wipe kills all your creatures simultaneously.

options.text: Blood Artist always resolves first
You choose the order of your own simultaneous triggers
Triggers resolve by board position

scenarios.reveal: CR 603.3b: a player controlling multiple triggers that trigger simultaneously chooses their order on the stack.

scenarios.title: APNAP Politics
scenarios.board_state: 4-player pod. A player two seats away casts a symmetrical wrath. You and another opponent each have death triggers.

options.text: Active player's triggers stack first, then APNAP order
You choose to go first since asked
The wrath-caster decides all order

scenarios.reveal: Active player's triggers are put on the stack first, then each other player in turn order. Since the stack is LIFO, the last trigger added resolves first.

scenarios.title: Order of Operations
scenarios.board_state: Your creature has a +1/+1 counter and a regeneration shield already up. Opponent casts 'Destroy target creature. If it had a counter, its controller loses 2 life.'

options.text: Regeneration replaces destruction entirely, so the life-loss clause never triggers
Creature dies but you still lose 2 life
You choose whether to regenerate after damage is calculated

scenarios.reveal: Regeneration is a replacement effect that swaps out the destruction event. If the creature is never destroyed, the 'if it had a counter' check never resolves true.

scenarios.title: Layers Check
scenarios.board_state: You control a 2/2. You cast an Aura giving +2/+2. Opponent then sets its power/toughness to 1/1 until end of turn.

options.text: 3/3 — Aura resolved second, so it wins
1/1 — set effects always win regardless of order
3/3 — layer 7b (set) applies before 7c (+X/+X), regardless of timestamp

scenarios.reveal: CR 613: P/T-setting effects are layer 7b, +X/+X effects are layer 7c. 7b always applies first in the layer sequence, so the +2/+2 is added on top of the set 1/1 base, giving 3/3.

scenarios.title: The Fog Bluff
scenarios.board_state: 4-player pod, you're at 8 life, facing lethal combat damage. You hold 1 untapped land and a possible Fog effect.

options.text: Cast Fog immediately at declare attackers
Wait until just before damage is assigned
Hold priority and never cast it, bluffing

scenarios.reveal: Fog effects can be cast any time before damage; waiting until right before damage maximizes information with zero downside, since nothing about the attack changes your available window.

scenarios.title: The Redundant Counter
scenarios.board_state: You control Counterspell, counter an opponent's spell. A third player casts their own Counterspell targeting yours.

options.text: Your Counterspell is countered; original spell resolves
Your Counterspell resolves first since it was on the stack first
Both cancel and the original also fizzles

scenarios.reveal: LIFO: the newest Counterspell resolves first, countering yours. Since your Counterspell never resolves, the original spell it targeted resolves normally.

scenarios.title: Mana Abilities Skip the Stack
scenarios.board_state: You tap a land for mana in response to an opponent's spell.

options.text: The mana ability goes on the stack and can be responded to
Mana abilities resolve immediately and never use the stack
It only skips the stack if it's a basic land

scenarios.reveal: CR 605: mana abilities don't use the stack; they resolve immediately when activated and can't be countered or responded to.

scenarios.title: Sorcery Speed Window
scenarios.board_state: It's your opponent's combat phase. You want to cast a sorcery-speed enchantment.

options.text: You can cast it now since you have priority
You must wait for your own main phase with an empty stack
You can cast it during any of your opponent's steps

scenarios.reveal: Sorcery-speed spells can only be cast during your main phase, when the stack is empty, and you have priority.

scenarios.title: Zero Toughness
scenarios.board_state: A resolving spell reduces a creature's toughness to 0. No one has priority yet.

options.text: It's destroyed as part of the spell's resolution
It's put into the graveyard by a state-based action before anyone gets priority
It stays until end of turn unless someone acts

scenarios.reveal: 0-toughness creatures die via state-based actions (CR 704.5f), checked immediately after a spell/ability finishes resolving, before any player receives priority.

scenarios.title: Legend Rule
scenarios.board_state: You control two copies of the same legendary creature (e.g., via a token copy).

options.text: You must sacrifice all but one immediately as an SBA
You may keep both since one is a token
Only the newer one survives automatically

scenarios.reveal: CR 704.5j: if a player controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name, that player chooses one to keep and puts the rest into their owners' graveyards as a state-based action.

scenarios.title: Fizzled Spell
scenarios.board_state: You cast removal targeting an opponent's creature. In response, they flicker it, and it returns as a new object.

options.text: Your spell still destroys the new object
Your spell has no legal target and is removed from the stack ('fizzles') without effect
You choose a new target

scenarios.reveal: A flickered creature is a new game object with no memory of being targeted. Since the original target no longer exists, the spell has no legal targets and is countered by the game rules on resolution.

scenarios.title: Can't Be Blocked vs Must Be Blocked
scenarios.board_state: You attack with a creature that 'can't be blocked except by two or more creatures.'

options.text: Opponent can block with exactly one creature
Opponent must either not block, or assign two-plus blockers
The creature is automatically unblockable

scenarios.reveal: This is a blocking restriction, not full evasion — the defending player may block with two or more creatures, or not block at all, but a single blocker is illegal.

scenarios.title: First Strike Damage Step
scenarios.board_state: Your first strike creature blocks a normal creature.

options.text: Both deal damage simultaneously
First strike creature deals damage in a separate, earlier combat damage step
First strike only matters if attacking, not blocking

scenarios.reveal: CR 510.4: if any creature has first or double strike, there are two combat damage steps. First strike (and double strike) creatures deal damage in the first step; if the normal creature survives, it deals damage in the second step.

scenarios.title: Deathtouch and Lethal Damage
scenarios.board_state: A 1/1 deathtouch creature blocks a 6/6 attacker.

options.text: The 6/6 needs to assign all 6 damage to the blocker to kill it
Any nonzero damage from a deathtouch source is considered lethal
Deathtouch only matters when attacking

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.2c: damage dealt by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal regardless of amount, which matters heavily for trample damage assignment math.

scenarios.title: Trample Plus Deathtouch
scenarios.board_state: A 4/4 with trample and deathtouch attacks into a 1/1 blocker. Attacker's controller assigns damage.

options.text: Must assign at least 4 damage to the blocker before trampling over
May assign as little as 1 damage (lethal, due to deathtouch) to the blocker and trample the rest through
Trample and deathtouch can't combine

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.19e: when assigning combat damage from a trampling deathtouch source, any nonzero amount is considered lethal for assignment purposes, so as little as 1 damage can be assigned to the blocker and the rest tramples through.

scenarios.title: Protection From Blue
scenarios.board_state: Your creature has protection from blue. An opponent casts a blue Aura targeting it.

options.text: The Aura resolves fine, it just can't deal damage
The Aura spell has no legal target and fizzles
Protection only stops damage, not enchanting

scenarios.reveal: Protection covers DEBT: can't be Damaged, Enchanted/Equipped, Blocked, or Targeted by the protected-from quality. A blue Aura can't legally target it at all.

scenarios.title: Hexproof vs Shroud
scenarios.board_state: You want to target your own creature with a beneficial spell. It has hexproof.

options.text: You can't target it, hexproof blocks all targeting
You can target it — hexproof only stops opponents from targeting it
Hexproof and shroud work identically for this purpose

scenarios.reveal: Hexproof only prevents the permanent from being targeted by spells/abilities your opponents control. Shroud prevents targeting by anyone, including its own controller.

scenarios.title: Ward Trigger
scenarios.board_state: You target an opponent's creature with Ward {2} using removal. You don't pay the ward cost.

options.text: Your spell simply fails to be cast
Your spell is cast normally, then countered by ward's triggered ability unless you pay
You must pay ward before casting, like an additional cost

scenarios.reveal: Ward is a triggered ability: when the permanent becomes the target of a spell/ability an opponent controls, that spell/ability is countered unless its controller pays the ward cost. It triggers after targeting, not as a cost to target.

scenarios.title: Menace Requirement
scenarios.board_state: A creature with menace is attacking. Defending player has three untapped creatures.

options.text: Any single creature can block it
It can only be blocked by two or more creatures
Menace prevents blocking entirely

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.111: a creature with menace can't be blocked except by two or more creatures.

scenarios.title: Flash Timing
scenarios.board_state: It's your opponent's end step. You want to cast a creature with flash.

options.text: You can't, creatures only come in on your turn
You may cast it any time you could cast an instant
Flash only works during combat

scenarios.reveal: Flash lets you cast the spell any time you have priority and could legally cast an instant, not just at sorcery speed.

scenarios.title: One Land Per Turn
scenarios.board_state: You've already played a land this turn. You draw a card that lets you play an additional land.

options.text: You're capped at one land per turn regardless
An effect granting extra land plays lets you exceed the normal limit
You'd need to wait until next turn

scenarios.reveal: The 'one land per turn' rule is a default that specific card effects can explicitly override by granting additional land drops.

scenarios.title: Kicker Is Optional
scenarios.board_state: You cast a spell with kicker but choose not to pay the kicker cost.

options.text: The spell can't be cast unless kicked
The spell resolves normally without the kicked effects
You must announce kicker before knowing if you can pay

scenarios.reveal: Kicker is always optional; you decide whether to pay it as part of casting, and the spell resolves with or without the extra effects accordingly.

scenarios.title: Flashback Doesn't Change Zone Rules
scenarios.board_state: You cast a sorcery with flashback from your graveyard, then it resolves.

options.text: It returns to your graveyard as normal for a resolved sorcery
It's exiled instead of going to the graveyard, per flashback's rule
It returns to your hand

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.34: flashback spells are exiled instead of going to the graveyard as they resolve (or are countered), which is why you can't flashback the same card twice.

scenarios.title: Cascade Doesn't Let You Choose Freely
scenarios.board_state: You cast a spell with cascade. You exile cards until you hit a nonland card with lower mana value.

options.text: You may cast any exiled card for free
You may cast the first nonland card revealed with lower mana value, or put it in hand
You must cast every card you flip regardless of cost

scenarios.reveal: Cascade exiles cards until the first nonland card with lower mana value is revealed; you may cast that specific card for free (or decline and put it in hand). The rest go to the bottom of your library in a random order.

scenarios.title: Declare Blockers Trigger Timing
scenarios.board_state: You control a creature with 'whenever this creature blocks, it gets +1/+1.' It blocks an attacker.

options.text: The bonus applies before blockers are even declared
The trigger goes on the stack after blockers are declared, and players get priority before damage
The bonus only applies retroactively after damage

scenarios.reveal: 'Blocks' triggers fire as part of the declare blockers step; they're put on the stack and resolve before combat damage is calculated, since players get priority in that step.

scenarios.title: Multiple Blockers, Damage Assignment Order
scenarios.board_state: Your attacker is blocked by two creatures. You must decide damage assignment order.

options.text: Damage is split evenly regardless
You announce a damage assignment order for the blockers, and must assign lethal to the first before moving to the next
The defending player decides how your damage is split

scenarios.reveal: CR 509.2 / 510.1c: the attacking player announces damage assignment order among multiple blockers and must assign at least lethal damage to an earlier blocker before assigning any to the next.

scenarios.title: Plus/Minus Counter Annihilation
scenarios.board_state: A creature has two +1/+1 counters and gets three -1/-1 counters added.

options.text: Counters just add up separately, net -3/-3 and -2/-2 base modifiers both apply
They annihilate in pairs as a state-based action, leaving one -1/-1 counter
Only the newest counters remain

scenarios.reveal: CR 704.5q: if a permanent has both +1/+1 and -1/-1 counters, N of each are removed as a state-based action until it has only one kind left. 2 and 3 counters cancel to leave one -1/-1 counter.

scenarios.title: Additional Cost vs Alternative Cost
scenarios.board_state: A spell says 'You may cast this for {2} rather than its mana cost' and separately 'As an additional cost, sacrifice a creature.'

options.text: Choosing the alternative cost skips the additional cost too
Additional costs still apply even when paying an alternative cost
You can only pay one type of cost modification per spell ever

scenarios.reveal: CR 601.2f: additional costs are paid regardless of whether you use the spell's normal mana cost or an alternative cost — the two stack unless the card says otherwise.

scenarios.title: Passing Priority Doesn't End the Turn
scenarios.board_state: You pass priority and your opponent also passes with an empty stack.

options.text: The turn ends immediately
The game moves to the next step/phase
Nothing happens; players must act again

scenarios.reveal: When all players pass priority in succession with the stack empty, the current step or phase ends and the game moves to the next one (or resolves the top stack object if not empty).

scenarios.title: Control-Changing Before Text-Changing
scenarios.board_state: An effect changes control of a creature (layer 2). Another effect changes its name/text (layer 3).

options.text: Text-changing effects are always applied first regardless of layer
Control-change (layer 2) is applied before text-change (layer 3), per layer order
They apply simultaneously

scenarios.reveal: CR 613.1: the layer system applies effects in a fixed order — control-changing effects (layer 2) before text-changing effects (layer 3) — regardless of timestamp.

scenarios.title: Timestamp Within the Same Layer
scenarios.board_state: Two static effects in layer 6 (ability-adding) both apply to the same creature, granting conflicting abilities.

options.text: Whichever effect started existing more recently (later timestamp) applies last, on top
The stronger card always wins
They're applied in alphabetical order

scenarios.reveal: CR 613.6: within the same layer (and sublayer), effects are applied in timestamp order — the order the objects generating them started existing — unless a dependency exists.

scenarios.title: Dependency Breaks Timestamp Order
scenarios.board_state: Effect A changes a creature's color to blue. Effect B says 'if this creature is blue, it gets +2/+2,' and both are static effects with A applied first by timestamp already.

options.text: Effect B is applied strictly by timestamp, ignoring A
Effect B depends on Effect A's result, so it's applied after A regardless of timestamp
Dependency doesn't affect layer application order

scenarios.reveal: CR 613.8: when one effect's result depends on another applying first (dependency), the dependent effect is applied after the one it depends on, even if timestamp order would suggest otherwise.

scenarios.title: Commander Tax
scenarios.board_state: Your commander has died and returned to the command zone twice already. You want to recast it a third time.

options.text: It still costs its normal mana cost
It costs {2} more for each previous time it was cast from the command zone, so {4} more total
The tax resets each game turn

scenarios.reveal: CR 903.8: each time a commander is cast from the command zone, its cost increases by {2} for each previous cast from that zone this game — cumulative, not reset per turn.

scenarios.title: Commander Damage Threshold
scenarios.board_state: An opponent's commander has dealt you 19 combat damage total across the game. It deals 2 more.

options.text: Nothing special happens until 21+ in a single hit
You lose the game — 21+ cumulative combat damage from a single commander is a loss condition
Commander damage resets each turn

scenarios.reveal: CR 903.10a: a player that has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses. Damage accumulates across turns, not per instance.

scenarios.title: Color Identity Includes Card Text
scenarios.board_state: You want to include a card with a red mana symbol only in its reminder text (not cost or characteristic-defining ability) in a non-red Commander deck.

options.text: Reminder text mana symbols don't count toward color identity
Any red symbol anywhere on the card makes it red for color identity
Color identity is only based on the card's color, not symbols

scenarios.reveal: CR 903.4: color identity includes mana symbols in the cost and rules text, but explicitly excludes reminder text and the color indicator's flavor-only elements where noted.

scenarios.title: Partner Commanders
scenarios.board_state: You want two different legendary creatures with 'Partner' as your commanders.

options.text: Not allowed, you can only ever have one commander
Allowed — both can be designated as commanders, each starting in the command zone separately
Only allowed if they share a color identity

scenarios.reveal: CR 903.7f: a player may designate two commanders if both have partner (or a compatible partner mechanic), each functioning as an independent commander.

scenarios.title: Choosing Targets in APNAP Order
scenarios.board_state: A spell you control requires each player to choose a target creature they control, resolving in a 4-player pod.

options.text: Only the caster chooses; others are random
Each affected player chooses in APNAP order as the spell resolves
All players choose simultaneously and secretly always

scenarios.reveal: When multiple players must make choices as part of a spell/ability resolving, they do so in APNAP order: active player first, then each nonactive player in turn order.

scenarios.title: Simultaneous Triggers Across Players
scenarios.board_state: A board wipe kills creatures controlled by three different players at once, each with a death trigger.

options.text: All three go on the stack in one player's choice of order
Active player's triggers go on stack first, then each nonactive player in turn order adds theirs
Triggers are ignored if they happen simultaneously across players

scenarios.reveal: APNAP governs the order triggers are placed on the stack when multiple players have triggers from the same event: active player first, then turn order for the rest.

scenarios.title: London Mulligan Basics
scenarios.board_state: You mulligan once, drawing a fresh 7-card hand.

options.text: You keep all 7 and just move on
You draw 7 then put 1 card on the bottom of your library, since you've mulliganed once
You draw only 6 cards for a single mulligan

scenarios.reveal: Under the London mulligan, you always draw a fresh 7, then put N cards on the bottom of your library equal to the number of times you've mulliganed.

scenarios.title: Loyalty Ability Timing
scenarios.board_state: You want to activate a planeswalker's loyalty ability for the second time this turn.

options.text: Allowed, as long as it's a different ability
Not allowed — only one loyalty ability per planeswalker per turn, and only at sorcery speed
Allowed at instant speed as many times as you have mana

scenarios.reveal: CR 606.3: a player may activate a loyalty ability of a permanent they control only any time they could cast a sorcery, and only once per planeswalker per turn.

scenarios.title: Redirecting Combat Damage to a Planeswalker
scenarios.board_state: You attack a planeswalker your opponent controls. The opponent blocks with a creature.

options.text: Damage still goes to the planeswalker since that's what you declared as attacking target
If blocked, combat damage from the attacker goes to the blocking creature, not the planeswalker
Damage is split between the blocker and the planeswalker

scenarios.reveal: When an attacking creature is blocked, its combat damage is assigned to the blocking creature(s), not to the planeswalker it was originally attacking — blocking redirects the damage.

scenarios.title: Instant Speed Response to a Trigger
scenarios.board_state: An opponent's ETB trigger is on the stack. You have an instant that could remove the creature that caused it.

options.text: Removing the creature now also removes the trigger from the stack
The trigger stays on the stack and resolves independently, even if the source creature is gone
You can't respond to a triggered ability

scenarios.reveal: Once a triggered ability is on the stack, it's independent of its source; removing the source doesn't remove the trigger unless the ability specifically checks for the source's continued existence ('intervening if' clauses aside).

scenarios.title: Split Second
scenarios.board_state: An opponent casts a spell with split second. You want to respond with an instant.

options.text: You may respond as normal
You can't cast spells or activate most abilities while it's on the stack
Split second only blocks counterspells specifically

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.61: while a spell with split second is on the stack, players can't cast spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities.

scenarios.title: Copying a Spell Doesn't Use the Stack Twice for Mana
scenarios.board_state: You copy an opponent's spell with a Twincast-style effect. The copy is now on the stack.

options.text: You must pay the spell's mana cost again for the copy
The copy is created directly on the stack, with no cost paid and it wasn't cast
The copy replaces the original entirely

scenarios.reveal: CR 706.2: copying a spell puts the copy directly onto the stack; it isn't cast, so no costs are paid, and effects that care about 'casting' don't trigger from the copy.

scenarios.title: Can't Be Countered Applies to the Copy Too
scenarios.board_state: You copy a spell that says 'this spell can't be countered.'

options.text: The copy loses that protection since it wasn't cast
The copy retains the printed characteristic and also can't be countered
Only the original is protected

scenarios.reveal: A copy has all the copiable values of the original, including abilities like 'can't be countered,' so it retains that protection even though it wasn't cast.

scenarios.title: Double Strike Damage Steps
scenarios.board_state: Your double strike creature is blocked by a creature without first strike.

options.text: It deals damage once, but doubled
It deals damage in both the first-strike and regular combat damage steps
Double strike only works when unblocked

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.4: a creature with double strike deals combat damage in the first strike step and again in the regular combat damage step, effectively hitting twice.

scenarios.title: Illegal Target at Cast Time
scenarios.board_state: You try to cast a removal spell targeting a creature with hexproof.

options.text: You may cast it and it just fails to do anything
You can't cast the spell at all — no legal target exists
You cast it targeting yourself instead automatically

scenarios.reveal: A spell needing a target can't be cast unless a legal target is available at the time of casting; hexproof removes it from your pool of legal targets.

scenarios.title: Multiple Replacement Effects, Same Event
scenarios.board_state: A creature entering the battlefield is affected by two different 'enters tapped' vs 'enters with a counter' replacement effects from different sources.

options.text: Both effects are automatically applied in an arbitrary fixed order
The affected object's controller chooses the order the replacement effects apply
Only one can ever apply; the other is ignored

scenarios.reveal: CR 616.1: when multiple replacement effects would apply to the same event, the affected object's controller (or its owner if it has none) chooses the order they apply in, and all of them can apply if they don't conflict.

scenarios.title: Prevention Effects Are Also Replacement
scenarios.board_state: You have 'prevent the next 3 damage that would be dealt to you this turn.' A creature deals 5 damage to you.

options.text: All 5 damage is prevented
3 damage is prevented, you take the remaining 2
The prevention shield doesn't apply to combat damage

scenarios.reveal: Damage prevention shields are replacement effects with a set amount; once that amount is used up (here, 3), any excess damage is dealt normally.

scenarios.title: Aura With No Legal Attachment
scenarios.board_state: An Aura is attached to a creature. The creature gains protection from the Aura's color.

options.text: The Aura stays attached, just doesn't affect it
The Aura becomes illegally attached and is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action
The creature is destroyed instead

scenarios.reveal: CR 704.5m: an Aura attached to an illegal object/player (e.g., due to newly gained protection) is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action.

scenarios.title: Convoke Taps Creatures, Not Mana
scenarios.board_state: You cast a spell with convoke and tap two creatures to help pay for it.

options.text: Each tapped creature reduces the cost by {1} generic or one mana of its color
Tapped creatures must exactly match the spell's colors
Convoke only reduces generic costs, never colored ones

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.51: for convoke, tap an untapped creature you control to pay {1} or one mana of any color that creature could produce (matching its color) toward the cost.

scenarios.title: Delve Exiles From Graveyard
scenarios.board_state: You cast a spell with delve and exile 3 cards from your graveyard to pay part of its cost.

options.text: Those cards go to exile permanently as part of the cost
They return to your graveyard after the spell resolves
Delve requires exiling cards from your hand instead

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.90: delve lets you exile cards from your graveyard to pay {1} generic mana each; this is a cost, so it's paid before the spell resolves and is not reversible.

scenarios.title: Attacking Doesn't Require Tapping If Vigilance
scenarios.board_state: You attack with a creature that has vigilance.

options.text: It taps as normal when declared as an attacker
It remains untapped and can still block later
Vigilance only works on defense

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.20: vigilance means the creature isn't tapped when declared as an attacker, so it stays available to block in future combats.

scenarios.title: Companion Isn't Automatically in Your Deck
scenarios.board_state: You have a Companion card sitting in a sideboard-like zone at game start.

options.text: It starts in your hand for free
It's not part of your deck; you may pay its cost plus {3} to put it into your hand once its companion condition is verified
It's automatically your commander

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.139: a companion begins the game in a separate zone; if its companion condition was met at deck construction, its owner may pay its mana cost plus {3} once per game to put it into their hand.

scenarios.title: Storm Copies
scenarios.board_state: You cast your third spell of the turn with storm.

options.text: You get 3 copies
You get copies equal to the number of spells cast before this one this turn — 2 copies
Storm counts all spells cast this game

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.39: storm creates a copy of the spell for each spell cast before it this turn (not including itself), so being the 3rd spell means 2 storm copies.

scenarios.title: Adventure Zone Change
scenarios.board_state: You cast the Adventure (instant/sorcery) side of a creature card with Adventure. It resolves.

options.text: It goes to the graveyard normally afterward, unable to be recast as a creature later
It's exiled instead, and can later be cast as the creature from exile
Adventure cards can only ever be cast as creatures

scenarios.reveal: CR 715: casting the Adventure side sends the card to exile instead of the graveyard upon resolution, allowing its owner to cast it later as the creature side from exile.

scenarios.title: Suspend Timing
scenarios.board_state: You suspend a spell with 3 time counters. Each of your upkeeps, one is removed.

options.text: You cast it for free the moment the counters hit zero, without using the stack
When the last counter is removed, you cast it for free — no mana cost, but timing restrictions like sorcery-speed-only cards can still not be cast at instant speed unless they have flash
Suspended cards are cast during your draw step automatically

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.61 (suspend): when the last time counter is removed, the card is cast without paying its mana cost, but normal timing restrictions for that card type still apply unless it has flash or the ability grants it.

scenarios.title: Zero or Less Loyalty
scenarios.board_state: A planeswalker's loyalty is reduced to 0 by combat damage.

options.text: It's destroyed immediately by the damage itself
It's put into the graveyard by a state-based action once loyalty hits 0
It stays with 0 loyalty until end of turn

scenarios.reveal: CR 704.5i: a planeswalker with loyalty 0 is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action, checked continuously, not as a direct result of the damage event itself.

scenarios.title: Unblocked Creature Must Deal Damage to Defending Player
scenarios.board_state: Your creature attacks and isn't blocked.

options.text: You may redirect its damage to any player
It deals combat damage to the player or planeswalker it's attacking
Unblocked attackers deal no damage unless stated

scenarios.reveal: An unblocked attacking creature deals its combat damage to the player or planeswalker it was declared as attacking, by default.

scenarios.title: Background Enchantments

scenarios.title: Planeswalker Damage Removes Loyalty Counters
scenarios.board_state: An unblocked attacking creature with power 4 is attacking a planeswalker with 6 loyalty counters.

options.text: You lose 4 life instead, since the planeswalker absorbed the attack
4 loyalty counters are removed from the planeswalker; no life is lost
The planeswalker is destroyed outright regardless of loyalty total

scenarios.reveal: CR 306.9: damage dealt to a planeswalker causes that many loyalty counters to be removed from it, rather than causing life loss.

scenarios.title: Planeswalkers Aren't Creatures
scenarios.board_state: An opponent casts 'Destroy target creature,' trying to target your planeswalker.

options.text: It's a legal target, since planeswalkers can be attacked like creatures
It's not a legal target — planeswalkers aren't creatures unless something specifically makes them one
It's legal only if the planeswalker is at 0 loyalty

scenarios.reveal: CR 306.2: planeswalkers are their own card/permanent type. Effects that say 'creature' don't affect planeswalkers unless the planeswalker has also become a creature some other way.

scenarios.title: Attacking a Specific Planeswalker
scenarios.board_state: Your opponent controls two planeswalkers. You declare one of your creatures as an attacker.

options.text: Attacking automatically splits damage between the player and both planeswalkers
For each attacking creature, you choose whether it's attacking the player or one specific planeswalker (or battle) they control
You must attack the player; planeswalkers can only be targeted by spells, not attacked

scenarios.reveal: CR 508.1: as attackers are declared, each attacking creature is assigned to attack the defending player or one planeswalker/battle that player controls — never more than one, and never split automatically.

scenarios.title: Two Planeswalkers, Same Name
scenarios.board_state: You control two planeswalkers with the exact same name.

options.text: Nothing happens — planeswalkers can duplicate freely
All planeswalkers are legendary, so the legend rule applies: you choose one to keep and put the rest into the graveyard
They automatically merge into one planeswalker with combined loyalty

scenarios.reveal: CR 704.5j (the legend rule): since 2017, every planeswalker card has the legendary supertype. If you control two or more legendary permanents with the same name, you keep one and the rest go to the graveyard as a state-based action.

scenarios.title: Cloning Doesn't Copy Counters or Auras
scenarios.board_state: You clone a creature that currently has three +1/+1 counters and an Aura attached.

options.text: The copy also has the 3 counters and the Aura
The copy has only the printed, copiable characteristics of the original — not its counters, attached Auras, or other non-copiable effects
The copy gets the Aura but not the counters

scenarios.reveal: CR 706.2: a copy effect copies only the copiable values of the object (essentially its printed characteristics as modified by other copy effects), never counters, Auras/Equipment attached to it, or other markers.

scenarios.title: Copying a Token Makes Another Token
scenarios.board_state: You control a token creature. An effect creates a copy of it.

options.text: The copy is a normal, non-token permanent since only the original was ever a token
The copy is also a token, since token status is part of what gets copied
Tokens can't be copied at all

scenarios.reveal: Copy effects preserve the fact that the source was a token, so the resulting copy is a token as well and follows the normal rule that tokens cease to exist once they leave the battlefield.

scenarios.title: Copies Keep the Value of X
scenarios.board_state: You cast a spell with X in its cost, paying X=5. In response, another spell copies it.

options.text: The copy has X=0, since no mana was paid for it
The copy has the same value of X (5) that the original spell had when it was cast
You choose a new value of X for the copy when it's created

scenarios.reveal: The value of X is locked in as a characteristic of the spell when it's cast (CR 601.2h) and carries over to any copy of it (CR 707.2), even though the copy itself was never cast or paid for.

scenarios.title: You Can Copy Abilities Too
scenarios.board_state: An effect reads 'Copy target activated or triggered ability. You may choose new targets for the copy.' You use it on an opponent's activated ability on the stack.

options.text: Only spells can be copied, not abilities
Activated and triggered abilities on the stack can be copied using the same rules that govern copying spells
Copying an ability requires paying its activation cost again

scenarios.reveal: CR 707 (Copying Objects) applies to spells, permanents, and abilities on the stack alike — copy effects aren't limited to spells.

scenarios.title: Protection Prevents Equipping Too
scenarios.board_state: You try to attach an Equipment to a creature that has protection from artifacts.

options.text: It equips fine — protection only stops spells
The creature can't become equipped by that Equipment — the equip ability has no legal target
It equips, but the Equipment's bonuses don't apply

scenarios.reveal: Protection is DEBT: can't be Damaged, Enchanted/Equipped, Blocked, or Targeted by the protected-from quality. An artifact Equipment can't legally attach to (or even target, for the equip ability) a creature with protection from artifacts.

scenarios.title: Protection From Everything Covers All Colors and More
scenarios.board_state: A creature has protection from everything.

options.text: It's only protected from colored spells
It can't be damaged, enchanted/equipped, blocked, or targeted by anything at all, regardless of color or type
It's still a legal target for colorless spells

scenarios.reveal: 'Protection from everything' is the broadest protection variant: DEBT applies against every possible source, not just colors.

scenarios.title: Protection Doesn't Save You From Sacrifice
scenarios.board_state: Your creature has protection from black. An opponent casts a black spell: 'Each player sacrifices a creature.'

options.text: Your creature is safe from being sacrificed because it has protection from black
Protection doesn't help — it's not damage, enchanting/equipping, blocking, or targeting, so you still have to choose a creature to sacrifice
You automatically sacrifice a different creature instead if you have one

scenarios.reveal: Protection only covers DEBT. A forced sacrifice is none of those, so a protected creature is not immune to it — if it's your only creature, it's the one you sacrifice.

scenarios.title: Graveyard Targets Can Also Disappear
scenarios.board_state: You cast a spell targeting a specific card in your graveyard to return it to hand. In response, an opponent exiles that card from your graveyard.

options.text: Your spell resolves and returns a different card from your graveyard instead
Your spell has no legal target left and doesn't resolve
Your spell still returns the card, wherever it currently is

scenarios.reveal: CR 608.2b: targets are rechecked on resolution. A card in the graveyard is just as much a target as anything else — if it leaves that zone before resolution, the spell has no legal target and doesn't resolve.

scenarios.title: Unearth Returns a Creature Temporarily
scenarios.board_state: You cast a creature from your graveyard using Unearth. It resolves and enters the battlefield.

options.text: It stays under your control permanently, just like a normal casting
It's exiled if it would leave the battlefield, and is exiled automatically at the beginning of the next end step if it's still around
It returns to the graveyard, not exile, whenever it leaves the battlefield

scenarios.reveal: Unearth grants a temporary reanimation: the creature is exiled instead of going to any other zone when it would leave the battlefield, and is exiled outright at the next end step if nothing else happened to it first.

scenarios.title: Optional Replacement Effects Let You Choose
scenarios.board_state: A permanent you control says 'If a source would deal damage to you, you may prevent that damage instead.' A spell deals 3 damage to you.

options.text: The damage is automatically prevented every time, since the effect exists
You choose whether to apply the replacement effect at the moment the event would happen; if you decline, the damage is dealt normally
You must decide before the damage-dealing spell even resolves

scenarios.reveal: CR 616.1: a replacement effect that says 'may' gives its controller a choice, made as the event it would replace is about to happen — not earlier and not automatically.

scenarios.title: Multiple Targets Must Each Be Legal
scenarios.board_state: You cast 'Destroy up to two target creatures,' targeting two creatures. In response, one of them becomes hexproof against you.

options.text: The whole spell fails to resolve since one target became illegal
The spell still resolves and does as much as it can — it destroys the remaining legal target and ignores the illegal one
You get to choose a new target to replace the illegal one

scenarios.reveal: CR 608.2b: a spell or ability with multiple targets is countered by the game rules only if ALL of its targets are illegal on resolution. If some remain legal, it resolves, affecting only those.

scenarios.title: Set P/T Beats Timestamp, But Not Counters
scenarios.board_state: A static ability sets your creature's power and toughness to 0/0 (layer 7b). It also has two +1/+1 counters (layer 7c).

options.text: Its final P/T is 0/0 — counters do nothing since the set effect is applied later
7b (set P/T) always applies before 7c (counters) regardless of timestamp, so the counters add on top of the set value — final P/T is 2/2
Whichever effect has the more recent timestamp wins entirely

scenarios.reveal: CR 613: within layer 7, sublayers are applied in fixed order (7a CDAs, 7b set P/T, 7c counters, 7d switch) regardless of timestamp. Set effects in 7b always resolve before counters in 7c get to modify the result.

scenarios.title: Dependency Breaks the Timestamp Tie
scenarios.board_state: Effect A (newer timestamp) turns your creature into a Human. Effect B (older timestamp) says 'Humans you control get +2/+2.'

options.text: B has the older timestamp, so it's already 'locked in' before A makes the creature a Human — no bonus
B depends on A (whether the creature counts as a Human depends on A having applied), so B is applied after A despite its older timestamp — the creature gets +2/+2
Only the newest effect in a layer ever applies; older ones are ignored

scenarios.reveal: CR 613.8: when whether or how one effect applies depends on another effect having applied first, the dependent effect is applied afterward, overriding normal timestamp order.

scenarios.title: Split Second Doesn't Stop Triggers Already Waiting
scenarios.board_state: You control a permanent with 'Whenever a player casts a spell, that player loses 1 life.' An opponent casts a spell with split second.

options.text: Your triggered ability can never go on the stack — split second locks the stack entirely
Split second only stops players from casting spells or activating non-mana abilities; your triggered ability still triggers and goes on the stack normally, above the split-second spell
Your trigger is skipped entirely for that spell

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.61: split second stops players from casting spells or activating abilities, but it doesn't stop triggered abilities from triggering and being put on the stack.

scenarios.title: One Regeneration Shield, One Save
scenarios.board_state: Your creature has a regeneration shield up. It's dealt lethal damage and is saved (tapped, removed from combat, damage removed). Later the same turn, it would be destroyed again.

options.text: The shield is still up and saves it again for free
That shield was used up; without activating regenerate again, the creature is destroyed for real this time
Regeneration shields never expire once created

scenarios.reveal: CR 701.16: regenerating a permanent consumes that shield. Each separate destroy event needs its own available shield to be replaced.

scenarios.title: Cloning Your Own Legendary Creature Triggers the Legend Rule
scenarios.board_state: You control a legendary creature. You clone it, becoming a copy with the same name.

options.text: Nothing happens — clones are exempt from the legend rule
You now control two legendary permanents with the same name — as a state-based action, you choose one to keep and put the other in the graveyard
The clone simply fails to copy the name to avoid the conflict

scenarios.reveal: CR 704.5j: the legend rule cares only about matching names among legendary permanents you control, regardless of how the duplicate name arose.

scenarios.title: Indestructible Doesn't Save a 0-Toughness Creature
scenarios.board_state: Your creature is indestructible. It gets -5/-5 from an effect, dropping its toughness to 0 or less.

options.text: It survives since it's indestructible
Indestructible only ignores destruction from lethal damage and 'destroy' effects — 0-or-less toughness still puts it into the graveyard as a state-based action
Indestructible prevents toughness from ever changing

scenarios.reveal: CR 704.5f and CR 702.12b: 0-or-less toughness is its own state-based action, unaffected by indestructible, which only stops destruction from damage or 'destroy' effects.

scenarios.title: No Destruction, No 'Dies' Trigger
scenarios.board_state: Your creature has 'Whenever this creature dies, draw a card' and is also indestructible. An opponent casts 'Destroy target creature' targeting it.

options.text: It draws you a card since the destroy spell resolved
Indestructible stops the destruction — the creature never dies, so the trigger never fires
The trigger fires, but the draw itself is prevented by indestructible

scenarios.reveal: 'Dies' means 'is put into a graveyard from the battlefield' (CR 700.4). Since indestructible prevents that from happening here, there's no death for the trigger to fire from.

scenarios.title: Ninjutsu Can Remove a Spell's Only Target
scenarios.board_state: An opponent casts removal targeting your attacking creature. In response, you use Ninjutsu to return that attacker to hand and put a ninja onto the battlefield attacking.

options.text: The removal spell automatically retargets the new ninja
The targeted creature is gone; the spell has no legal target left and doesn't resolve
Ninjutsu can't be used in response to a spell targeting the attacker

scenarios.reveal: CR 608.2b: Ninjutsu returns the original attacker before the removal spell resolves, so its only target no longer exists. Spells can't retarget themselves — it simply fails to resolve.

scenarios.title: Independent 'May' Triggers From Different Players
scenarios.board_state: Two creatures controlled by different players die simultaneously. Each has 'Whenever this creature dies, its controller may draw a card and lose 1 life.'

options.text: Both players must make the same choice
APNAP determines whose trigger goes on the stack first, but each player independently chooses yes or no for their own trigger
Only the active player's trigger exists; the other is ignored

scenarios.reveal: CR 603.3b/101.4: simultaneous triggers controlled by different players are ordered APNAP for stacking, but each triggered ability's optional choice is made independently by its own controller.

scenarios.title: One Target, Total Fizzle
scenarios.board_state: You cast 'Destroy target creature. You gain 2 life' (a single target). In response, that creature gains protection from the spell's color, making the target illegal.

options.text: The spell still resolves for the life gain, just skips the destroy part
Since its only target is illegal, the entire spell doesn't resolve at all — no destruction and no life gain
You choose a new legal target to save the spell

scenarios.reveal: CR 608.2b: a spell with a single target that becomes illegal is countered by the game rules entirely. Compare a multi-target spell, where only the illegal targets are skipped and the rest still happens.

scenarios.title: Mana Abilities Still Work Under Split Second
scenarios.board_state: An opponent casts a spell with split second. You want to tap a land for mana.

options.text: You can't do anything, including tapping lands, until split second ends
Mana abilities don't use the stack and are explicitly exempt from split second's restriction — you can still tap for mana
You may only tap for colorless mana during split second

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.61: split second stops players from casting spells and activating abilities that aren't mana abilities. Mana abilities remain legal throughout.

scenarios.title: Choosing an Order That Doesn't Actually Matter
scenarios.board_state: A creature enters the battlefield as a copy of another creature (one replacement effect) and also enters tapped (a second, unrelated replacement effect).

options.text: You must apply 'enters tapped' first since it was set up earlier
You choose an order per the rules, but since the two effects don't interact, the result is identical either way — it's a copy, and it's tapped
Only one of the two replacement effects can actually apply

scenarios.reveal: CR 616.1 requires choosing an order for multiple applicable replacement effects, but that choice only matters when the effects could actually interact. Here they modify unrelated aspects, so the outcome doesn't change.

scenarios.title: First-Strike Damage Trigger Survives the Creature's Own Death
scenarios.board_state: Your creature has first strike and 'Whenever this creature deals combat damage, you gain 1 life.' It deals first-strike damage, and its non-first-strike, deathtouch blocker kills it back in the regular damage step.

options.text: The life-gain trigger never resolves since the creature died before the trigger left the stack
The trigger already went on the stack when first-strike damage was dealt and resolves independently, regardless of what happens to the creature afterward
The trigger is removed from the stack once its source leaves the battlefield

scenarios.reveal: Once a triggered ability is on the stack, it resolves on its own — it doesn't need its source to still exist (that's specifically the concern of leaves-the-battlefield/LKI abilities, and even those still resolve).

scenarios.title: Convoke: Color or Generic, Your Choice
scenarios.board_state: You cast a spell with convoke costing {2}{G}. You tap a green creature to help pay.

options.text: That creature can only pay the {G} in the cost, never the generic part
You choose — a green creature tapped for convoke can pay either the {G} or one of the generic mana
Convoke creatures can only ever pay generic costs

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.51: each creature tapped for convoke pays for {1} or one mana of any of its colors, controller's choice.

scenarios.title: Cascade Doesn't Make You Cast the Card
scenarios.board_state: You cast a spell with cascade. It exiles cards from your library until hitting a lower-mana-value nonland card.

options.text: You must cast that card for free, no choice involved
You may cast it without paying its mana cost, or decline — either way the rest of the exiled cards then go to the bottom of your library in a random order
All the exiled cards are cast for free

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.86: cascade lets you cast the revealed card without paying its mana cost — it's optional. The remaining exiled cards go to the bottom of your library in a random order regardless of your choice.

scenarios.title: Escape Needs Cards Besides Itself
scenarios.board_state: You want to cast a creature with Escape from your graveyard. Its escape cost requires exiling 2 other cards from your graveyard, but your graveyard only contains that creature card and nothing else.

options.text: You may pay the mana cost alone and skip the exile requirement
You can't cast it via escape right now — there aren't enough OTHER cards in the graveyard to exile
You exile itself twice to make up the difference

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.136: escape costs specify exiling a number of other cards from your graveyard, not the escaping card itself. Without enough of them available, the cost can't be paid.

scenarios.title: Partner Commanders Don't Legend-Rule Each Other
scenarios.board_state: You control two different legendary creatures, each with partner, as your commanders.

options.text: Since both are commanders, the legend rule forces you to sacrifice one
The legend rule only cares about matching names — two partners with different names never conflict
Partner permanents are entirely exempt from the legend rule under any circumstance

scenarios.reveal: CR 704.5j only triggers on matching legendary permanent names. Different partner commanders simply have different names — but note that's a 'different names' exemption, not a blanket partner exemption; two copies of the same partner legend would still conflict.

scenarios.title: Ward Triggers on Every New Targeting, Not Just Once
scenarios.board_state: A creature has Ward {2}. An opponent targets it with a spell and pays the ward cost. Later the same turn, a different opponent spell targets it again.

options.text: Ward has already been paid once this turn, so it doesn't trigger again
Ward triggers independently every time the permanent becomes the target of a new opponent spell or ability — it's not a once-per-turn effect
Ward only works against the first spell that ever targets it

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.21: ward's triggered ability triggers each time the permanent becomes the target of a spell or ability an opponent controls, with no limit on how many times per turn.

scenarios.title: Phasing Preserves Everything About a Permanent
scenarios.board_state: A creature with two +1/+1 counters and an attached Aura phases out, then phases back in on your next turn.

options.text: It comes back as a fresh permanent with no counters or Aura
It phases back in exactly as it was — counters, attached Auras/Equipment, and tapped status are unchanged, since phasing isn't a zone change
The Aura falls off during phasing since the creature technically leaves the battlefield

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.26: phased-out permanents aren't considered to have left the battlefield — everything about them, including counters and attachments, is preserved and simply treated as though it doesn't exist while phased out.

scenarios.title: A Doubled Trigger Gives You Two Separate Choices
scenarios.board_state: You control an effect that makes your triggered abilities trigger an additional time. Your permanent has 'Whenever you draw a card, you may pay {1}. If you do, gain 1 life.' You draw a card, causing the ability to trigger twice.

options.text: You make one choice that applies to both instances
Each instance of the doubled trigger is independent — you decide separately for each whether to pay {1} and gain the life
The second trigger is simply ignored as a duplicate

scenarios.reveal: Extra-trigger effects create genuinely separate instances of the triggered ability on the stack, each with its own independent choice.

scenarios.title: One Creature With Extra Blocks Still Can't Satisfy Menace
scenarios.board_state: An attacking creature has menace. The defending player controls a single creature with 'This creature can block an additional creature.'

options.text: That one creature can legally block the menace attacker alone, since it's allowed to block two creatures
Menace requires two or more DIFFERENT creatures to be declared as blockers — one creature's ability to block multiple attackers doesn't satisfy that, since it's still only one blocking creature
Menace is ignored once any creature has an additional-blocking ability

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.111: menace requires the attacking creature to be blocked by two or more creatures. A single creature — however many attackers it's allowed to block — still only counts as one blocker.

scenarios.title: Storm Copies Resolve Before the Original Spell
scenarios.board_state: You cast a spell with storm as the 3rd spell you've cast this turn. Its storm trigger creates 2 copies of it.

options.text: The copies are created and resolve at the same time as the original, as part of its resolution
The storm triggered ability goes on the stack above the spell itself; its copies are created and fully resolve before the original spell ever resolves
The copies wait on the stack until after the original spell resolves

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.39: storm triggers when you cast the spell, so the ability goes on the stack above it. Its copies resolve — and are gone — before the original spell gets its turn.

scenarios.title: Removing More Counters Than Exist
scenarios.board_state: Your creature has one -1/-1 counter. An effect says 'remove two -1/-1 counters from it.'

options.text: The effect fails entirely since there aren't two to remove
You simply remove the one that's there — you can't remove more counters than actually exist
The creature gains a +1/+1 counter to make up the difference

scenarios.reveal: You can never remove more counters of a kind than are actually present on a permanent — the effect just does as much as it can.

scenarios.title: Not Every Spell Needs a Target
scenarios.board_state: You cast a spell that reads 'Draw two cards.'

options.text: You must choose a target player for the draw
This spell doesn't say 'target' anywhere, so it needs no target at all — it just resolves and affects its caster
It automatically targets the caster and can be stopped by hexproof

scenarios.reveal: Only effects that literally say 'target' need one selected at cast time. Effects that just say 'you' or 'each player' resolve without any targeting step.

scenarios.title: Hexproof From a Specific Color
scenarios.board_state: Your creature has hexproof from blue. An opponent tries to target it with a black removal spell.

options.text: Hexproof from blue also blocks black spells, since it's still 'hexproof'
Hexproof from blue only stops blue sources from targeting it — a black spell can target it just fine
Hexproof from a color is the same as full hexproof

scenarios.reveal: Qualified hexproof ('hexproof from [quality]') only stops targeting by sources with that specific quality. It offers no protection from anything else.

scenarios.title: Planeswalkers Can't Block
scenarios.board_state: An opponent attacks you. You want your planeswalker to block the attacker.

options.text: Any planeswalker may be declared as a blocker
Planeswalkers aren't creatures, so they can't be declared as blockers unless something has turned them into a creature
Planeswalkers can block only attackers that are also targeting them

scenarios.reveal: Only creatures can be declared as blockers. A planeswalker that hasn't become a creature has no way to block.

scenarios.title: Turning a Permanent Into a Copy Doesn't Use the Stack
scenarios.board_state: You control a Clone-style creature that enters as a copy of another creature by way of a triggered ability.

options.text: The copy effect is itself cast as a new spell, using the stack
The copy effect just directly changes the permanent's copiable characteristics when its ability resolves — nothing new is cast
The original creature is exiled and a new one is cast in its place

scenarios.reveal: Copy effects for permanents change what a permanent IS, applied directly as the ability resolves — they don't 'cast' anything new.

scenarios.title: Foretell: Pay Now, Cast Later
scenarios.board_state: During your turn, you pay {2} and exile a card with foretell from your hand, face down.

options.text: You must cast it immediately or lose it
It stays exiled face down; on a later turn, you may cast it from exile for its foretell cost instead of its normal mana cost
Foretelling a card counts as casting it

scenarios.reveal: CR 702.128: foretelling exiles the card face down for {2} during your turn. You may later cast it from exile for its foretell cost — foretelling itself is not casting.

scenarios.title: Prevent Damage Doesn't Prevent Life Loss
scenarios.board_state: You have 'Prevent all damage that would be dealt to you this turn.' An opponent's spell says 'Each player loses 2 life.'

options.text: The prevention shield stops the life loss too
Losing life directly isn't damage — your prevention effect does nothing here, and you lose the 2 life
You only lose 1 life since prevention halves it

scenarios.reveal: Damage and life loss are different game concepts. A 'prevent damage' effect only replaces damage events — direct life-loss effects aren't damage and go through untouched.

scenarios.title: Each Opponent Draws — Whose Turn Is It to Resolve First?
scenarios.board_state: You cast a spell that says 'Each opponent draws a card' in a 4-player Commander game.

options.text: All three draws must be simultaneous, or the game breaks
The game still processes it in APNAP order, but since drawing a card involves no choice, the outcome is exactly the same regardless of order
Only the next player in turn order draws; the others don't

scenarios.reveal: CR 101.4: effects affecting multiple players are processed in APNAP order, but for a non-choice action like drawing a card, order doesn't change the outcome — it only matters when an order-dependent choice is involved.
